The status of the seven not accounted ⁠for ​yet is not immediately known. https://p.dw.com/p/5M5BF Skip next section Germany urges UN's top court to quash Israel genocide case 09/07/2026 September 7, 2026 Germany urges UN's top court to quash Israel genocide case Germany 's top legal representative has told the UN's top court that a genocide case over weapons sales to Israel , should be thrown out. The matter was brought by Nicaragua and Germany's top lawyer, Julia Monar, said the judges at the International Court of Justice lacked the jurisdiction to rule on the case , dismissing Nicaragua's allegations of Berlin "facilitating genocide" as "inaccurate and distorted." Nicaragua argues that Germany's backing of Israel, notably in terms of arms exports, contravenes the 1948 UN Genocide Convention. "Nicaragua’s conduct indicates that it was not interested in hearing Germany’s view on its allegations, but simply in bringing Germany before this court," Monar, told the judges. Monar said that Nicaragua failed to properly notify the German government and gave her country less than a month to reply before launching proceedings. It's typically expected that countries attempt to resolve disputes before bringing them to the court. Monar pointed out that Berlin scrutinizes all exports of military equipment in accordance with international law. "Germany has not, since 2024, authorized an export of weapons of war, with final destination in Israel that can be used in the Gaza conflict,” she said. The German government operates what it calls a "case by case" approval process of arms sales to Israel, with the stated goal of avoiding anything that might be used in Gaza , where at least 73,000 Palestinians were killed between the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks on Israeli civlians and late August of this year. However, Germany only instituted this policy in 2025, and continued to ship defensive equipment worth hundreds of millions of euros this year. https://p.dw.com/p/5M52u Skip next section Iran issues warning as South Korea mulls Hormuz contribution 09/07/2026 September 7, 2026 Iran issues warning as South Korea mulls Hormuz contribution Iran 's Foreign Ministry issued a warning against any country participating in security operations in the Strait of Hormuz . Baqaei noted Tehran's diplomatic relationship with Seoul, saying that Iran "places great importance on its friendly relations with the Republic of Korea." According to its latest figures, an average of 10 commodity vessels, transited the vital shipping route over the past 10 days. Kpler recorded the number on Sunday, which was down from the 15 vessels on Friday and the 13 seen on Saturday. The drop in maritime traffic comes amid strikes targeting tankers by the US and Iran. On Saturday, US forces hit three Iranian oil tankers, following Iranian attacks on US warships in the region. "Commercial tankers are now being deliberately used as instruments of reciprocal economic pressure, substantially weakening the previous distinction between military confrontation and commercial shipping," Marisks noted. Photograph: Lisa Nipp/AP View image in fullscreen Christa Pike pictured in 2002. Pike’s attorneys say she had an abusive childhood. Photograph: Lisa Nipp/AP Tennessee Tennessee to execute a woman for first time in 200 years after governor denies clemency Lawyers for Christa Pike, 50, convicted of killing classmate in Knoxville in 1995, ask supreme court to grant stay Abené Clayton and agencies Mon 28 Sep 2026 20.52 EDT First published on Mon 28 Sep 2026 18.54 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Christa Pike, a woman who was convicted of murder 30 years ago, is set to be put to death on Wednesday after her request for clemency was denied by Tennessee governor Bill Lee on Monday. If the execution goes through, she will be the first woman executed in the state in 200 years. Pike, who is now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend, who was 17 at the time, killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmate at Knoxville Job Corps in 1995. The case received widespread attention because of the brutality of the killing, the ages of the people involved, and because a satanic symbol was carved into the victim’s body. Pike was convicted of first-degree murder the following year and sentenced to death, making her the youngest woman to be put on death row in modern US history. Since her sentence, her history as a victim of sexual abuse and mental health challenges has come to light. As her execution date approached, civil rights groups like the ACLU and Amnesty International have called on the public to reach out to the governor’s office to ask that he take Pike off of death row. But Lee declined to halt her execution. “After deliberate consideration of Christa Gail Pike’s request for clemency and after a thorough review of the case, I am upholding the sentence of the State of Tennessee and do not plan to intervene,” he said in a statement . In response to Lee’s decision, Pike’s attorneys said that they were “deeply saddened and heartbroken” by the governor’s decision and that through this choice the state is dismissing decades of research about the amount of responsibility an 18-year-old – especially one with severe trauma – should bear for their criminal actions. “Throughout her childhood, Christa was failed by people and institutions that should have shown her care and meaningful intervention,” Pike’s attorneys said in a statement. “The 18-year-old girl suffering from severe mental illness and near-debilitating trauma no longer exists. Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions, receives proper treatment for her mental illness, and provides for and guides fellow incarcerated women.” Pike’s attorneys have also asked the supreme court to stay the execution. Assistant federal defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike was sexually abused starting from when she was a toddler and that she was raped at 11 and 17. He said Pike’s lawyers at the penalty phase of her trial did not present the jury with what he said was critical information about her past or argue that her age should be a consideration. Pike , who has never denied her role in Slemmer’s killing, was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. “I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime,” Pike said in a statement included in her clemency petition. Ferrell said more is known today about adolescent brain development and that Pike’s death sentence is an outlier. He noted that Pike’s boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, who was 17 at the time, was sentenced to life with the possibility of parole because of his age. He was denied parole last year. A third teen admitted to being an accessory and received probation. May Martinez, Slemmer’s mother, told the Associated press that her daughter volunteered with the Special Olympics, loved roller skating and wanted to pursue a career in computers. “She was easygoing. She was a computer geek to begin with. She and my husband would build and tear apart the computers constantly,” Martinez told the outlet. “She trusted everybody, and that was her downfall.” The last woman executed in Tennessee was in 1820, according to the Death Penalty Information Center . Martin Eve, charged with being an accessory to murder, was executed by hanging. Most recently, Missouri in 2023 executed Amber McLaughlin, a transgender woman, for a 2003 killing, in what is believed to be the first execution of a transgender woman in the US. In 2021, the federal government executed Lisa Montgomery, marking the first time in nearly seven decades that the US government has put a female inmate to death. Georgia executed a woman in 2015. Julius Windham visits a memorial on Sunday outside the home where authorities say a gunman killed multiple people, including Windham's daughter, in Erie, Pennsylvania. Photograph: Ted Shaffrey/AP View image in fullscreen Julius Windham visits a memorial on Sunday outside the home where authorities say a gunman killed multiple people, including Windham's daughter, in Erie, Pennsylvania. Photograph: Ted Shaffrey/AP Pennsylvania Pennsylvania shooter who killed eight was a grandfather, says slain child’s dad Father of toddler killed in Erie mass shooting says reported gunman never seemed distressed or out of the ordinary Coral Murphy Marcos and agencies Sun 11 Oct 2026 19.48 EDT Last modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 23.20 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The man who killed eight people, before turning the gun on himself, in a mass shooting in a home in Erie, Pennsylvania, on Friday was a grandfather who had not shown signs that he was capable of such violence, according to people who knew the shooter. A man whose toddler was among those killed said on Sunday that the man never seemed distressed or out of the ordinary, the Associated Press reports . “I think that was a front for him,” said Julius Windham during a memorial to victims of Friday’s shooting. Windham’s one-year-old daughter, Amarianna; her pregnant mother; and the woman’s five-year-old son and unborn baby were among the victims. “Him every day, him smiling and being just – you would think of nothing like that would happen,” Windham said. Nine people, including children, dead after mass shooting in Pennsylvania Read more The 45-year-old gunman took his own life. Authorities have not released his name, but the Erie police chief, Rick Lorah, said he was related to seven of the victims. The eighth was a friend of the pregnant woman, he said. Police have not made their names public, either. Mourners on Sunday placed candles, flowers and stuffed animals outside the home where the man opened fire shortly before 5 pm on Friday. Windham wore a T-shirt with pictures of the slain woman and children and the words “Forever in my heart”. “Words can’t even explain what I’m going through right now,” Windham said. “But I gotta be strong for my community, you know what I’m saying? My family, my daughters, my sons, everybody.” “We don’t want that dark memory to be what defines their lives in this world,” a family friend told Cleveland 19 News . “How do you even fathom something like this? How will you go home and tell your kids: ‘Hey, your mom, your siblings, your uncles and everybody else just got murdered by your grandpa?’” Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators included muffled gunshot sounds coming from inside the home just before two “distressed” women arrived and began pounding on the door, Lorah said. The gunman then came out and shot them before returning inside. View image in fullscreen Firefighters work outside the home where nine members of a family were killed in a mass shooting on Saturday in Erie, Pennsylvania. Photograph: Jeff Swensen/Getty Images Responding officers found the two women dead outside. After deploying a drone and robot, they went inside and found the bodies of the five-year-old boy and one-year-old girl on the first floor; two more women and two young men in a stairwell; and the shooter on the second floor. “Out of respect for the victims and the families, I will not discuss the details of what our officers encountered inside that home,” the chief said at a news conference . “But I want our community to understand the gravity of what happened and the profound impact this tragedy has had on those involved and on our community as a whole,” he said. Erie is about 120 miles (190km) north of Pittsburgh. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines US Get the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion Lorah declined to discuss motive but suggested mental health could be a factor. He said investigators would talk to relatives and examine the cellphones of the women who were killed outside the home. “They knew something was going on at that house,” Lorah said. “We have to figure out what that is.” Nicole and Debra Eller, whose best friend was among the victims, told the Associated Press they have known the family for more than 30 years. Nicole Eller said the shooter “was a good guy, and then he started going downhill with everything”. “They were a lovely family. Who would have thought this would ever happen?” Debra Eller said. “Oh my gosh, this is so upsetting. This should have never happened to her or the kids or anybody. His grandchildren, his kids, how can you do that?” The Erie shooting was reminiscent of a 1982 massacre in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, in which a man killed 13 people, including five of his own children. At a news conference on Saturday, Erie’s mayor, Daria Devlin, addressed a portion of her remarks directly to the victims’ families. “I am so deeply sorry,” Devlin said. What happened to you was horrific, and there is nothing that any of us can say today that will make this any easier ... Our entire community is with you, we’re grieving with you. And we are here to support you.” “My heart breaks for this family. Lori and I are praying for their loved ones and the entire Erie community,” said Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, in a post on X on Saturday.
